name: Sesarwa, language of the Tati Bushmen / Masarwas
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 6 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Dornan, Samuel Shaw (1917). The Tati Bushmen (Masarwas) and their Language. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 47: 37-112.
catalog_locator: p. 63, section 'The Noun' (page image the copy we hold = PDF page 98 of the archive.org DLI volume scan; scanned of); tones p. 61 (scanned)
catalog_quote: The great majority of words in Sesarwa end in a vowel, or in a nasal m̃ or ñ, and never in any other consonant. The accent falls on the last syllable of a word and the stress rises towards the end thus—Chìnă amă yà kakhŏ, chà ke kwă chà yowàhă = I shall bring you the pot, if you order me. This sounds rather strange to a European ear, but it is not unpleasant. [p. 63, 'The Noun'] ... There are at least three tones in the Sesarwa language, the high, middle and low. It is by these tones that words spelled the same way, meaning quite different things, are distinguished; for instance, hwee, to be surprised, is pronounced with the high tone, hwee, fear, with the middle, and hwee, to squeeze out pus, with the low. Similarly |gaa, |gaa and |gaa, meaning to lean on, effort, and a block of wood. [p. 61]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Northern Tshwa (tsoa1238) is not in the catalog and this search of works with stress in the title produced a single title hit, Hitchcock 1988 'Settlement, seasonality and subsistence stress among the Tyua of northern Botswana', which is an ethnographic chapter on seasonal food/subsistence stress (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as an ethnographic work; MASCA archaeology series) and irrelevant to word stress (priority none; not downloaded, archive.org copy is lending-only). To look for a first-hand prosody statement I downloaded the two open first-hand descriptions available: Phiri & Andrason 2022 'A Living Grammar Sketch of Tjwao' (Living Tongues, CC BY, 48 pp.) and Fehn & Phiri 2017 'Nominal marking in Northern Tshwa' (SPIL 48, OA). Both are silent on word stress; both treat the language as tonal (sketch p. 4: each vowel 'acts as a distinct tone-bearing unit'; Fehn & Phiri p. 107: 'lexical tone is distinctive in all Northern Tshwa varieties. we have therefore chosen not to mark tone'). No source read states where word stress falls, so no new stress statement was found. The only remaining candidate for a stress/tone statement is Phiri 2015 'Tshwao phoneme inventory' (UZ MA thesis, not online; ir.uz.ac.zw refused connection) — medium priority. new_statements.rule_in_words: Dornan (1917) describes the Tati Bushman language ('Sesarwa') as a three-tone language (high, middle, low; p. 61) and states that the accent falls on the final syllable of the word, with stress rising towards the end of the word/phrase (p. 63). Modern work (Phiri 2021; Phiri & Andrason 2022; Fehn & Phiri 2017) treats the language as tonal with the mora as tone-bearing unit and makes no stress statement at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The example sentence carries grave/breve/macron marks over vowels whose exact values are hard to read in the scan; Dornan does not explain them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('the last syllable of a word') illustrated with a whole sentence, so the 'stress rises towards the end' remark may describe phrase-level intonation. Century-old, impressionistic, pre-phonemic description by a missionary; no instrumental or phonological analysis. Tone marks are absent from the wordlists.
new_statements.identity_note: Dornan 1917 describes 'Sesarwa', the language of the Tati Bushmen (Masarwa) of the Tati/Sansokwe district of NE Botswana and the Bulawayo area; Glottolog files it under tsoa1238 and lists Tati, Masarwa, Sesarwa among the alternative names. Modern sources held by the project describe Tjwao (Tsholotsho, Zimbabwe; Phiri 2021, Phiri & Andrason 2022), several Northern Tshwa lects (Fehn & Phiri 2017) and 'Thabala Tchoe' (Pratchett 2020); none of them states a stress rule. Pratchett's Thabala Tchoe and Mathes's Tsua are Southern/other Tshwa lects and may belong to other glottocodes.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: All oral vowels can also be long or bimoraic, i.e., ii, uu, ee, oo, and aa. As is true of other Khoe languages, such long or bimoraic vowels are analyzed in Tjwao as two short vowels. This is because each vowel acts as a distinct tone-bearing unit.
sources.note: Silent on word stress: the sound-system chapter (§2 Vowels, Consonants) has no stress, accent or tone section; the only prosodic remark is that long vowels are two short vowels because each vowel is a tone-bearing unit (i.e., the language is treated as tonal). No statement of stress placement anywhere in the 48-page sketch (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).

sources.citation: Fehn, Anne-Maria & Admire Phiri (2017). Nominal marking in Northern Tshwa (Kalahari Khoe). Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics 48: 105-122. doi:10.5774/48-0-284 [already in per-language bibliography; not a works with stress in the title; read for a prosody statement]

sources.quote: While we acknowledge that lexical tone is distinctive in all Northern Tshwa varieties discussed in this article, more research will be needed to determine the exact number of distinctive tone levels and tone melodies; we have therefore chosen not to mark tone on the examples cited.
sources.note: Silent on stress; states that lexical tone is distinctive in all Northern Tshwa varieties (Tjwao, Hiechware, Gǁabak'e, Tcire-Tcire) but the tone system is undescribed, so tone is left unmarked. No mention of stress or accent.
